No.17

Making Peace With Oneself on the Long Road of Caregiving

Strength has its limits and money its end; while caring for others, we must also care for ourselves.

Author's record · translated; the Chinese original is authoritative

Open in reading mode →

🔶Inquiry to Ksitigarbha Bodhisattva

I asked Ksitigarbha Bodhisattva: could you teach how caregivers should adjust their state of mind when a family member needs long-term care, and what to do when the family's finances can no longer support long-term care?

🔶The Bodhisattva's Teaching

"Caring for the sick
is not one person's karma;
in a household of long illness,
first settle the heart.
When strength runs out,
compassion is not lost;
when money comes to an end,
family love is not abandoned.

To give all one's strength
is to have a clear conscience;
to know where to stop
is also wisdom.
Do not, because you cannot,
blame yourself as evil;
do not take a step back
and mistake it for running away."

🔶Plain Rendering

Caring for the sick has never been one person's responsibility alone. When a family member needs long-term care, first steady your own heart. A person's strength has times when it runs out; this does not mean you have lost compassion. A family's finances may reach a point of exhaustion; this does not mean you have abandoned your loved one. As long as you have done your best, your conscience is clear; knowing when to stop at the right time is also a kind of wisdom. Do not blame yourself as a bad person because you "cannot do more"; do not mistake "having to step back and look for other ways" for running away.

🔶Inquiry to Ksitigarbha Bodhisattva

I replied to Ksitigarbha Bodhisattva: I am slow to understand. Bodhisattva, you said "know where to stop". So how should we view caregivers who, unable to bear the pressure, kill or harm the person in their care, or end their own lives?

🔶The Bodhisattva's Teaching

"Theirs is not an evil heart;
it is a heart buried by suffering.
They do not wish to take life;
they cannot see a way.
When the strength of the heart is spent,
wisdom does not appear;
compassion, driven to the edge,
turns into harm.

This is not 'knowing where to stop';
it is 'losing the power to stop';
not stopping in clarity,
but breaking off in darkness.
Grieve for their suffering,
but do not praise their deeds;
protect the heart,
but do not take such deeds as the way."

🔶Plain Rendering

They (caregivers who act in extreme ways) do not act from malice; pain has completely covered their minds. They do not truly want to take a life; in the darkness they simply cannot see any other way out.

When a person's strength of heart is used up, wisdom cannot appear; compassion pushed to its limit turns, terribly, into harm.

This is not "the wisdom of knowing when to stop", but "a complete collapse while lost"; not clearly choosing to stop in the light, but cutting everything off in despair in the dark.

We should feel compassion for the suffering they bore, but not approve of what they did; we should think about how to protect people's hearts, and not treat such extreme acts as a solution to follow.
